title: Färs av kalvkött (Veal Forcemeat)
description: Prepared with veal, suet or beef or lard, and white pepper.

ingredients.name: 1 hg. dry, cleaned suet from beef or 1 hg. lard

steps: Dry the meat with a cloth wrung out in hot water, free it from sinews and membranes, cut it into dice and grind it 3 times through a meat grinder.
Chop the suet finely with a knife on a cutting board, mix it together with the seasonings with the veal forcemeat, which is ground an additional 3 times through the grinder.

Pound the forcemeat thereafter together with the flour in a stone mortar with a wooden pestle until it becomes even and smooth, then add the egg and egg yolks, one at a time, with continued vigorous pounding.
Pass the forcemeat through a hair sieve and let it stand in a cold place or on ice for several hours, or preferably until the following day.
Then work it vigorously with a spoon while the cream is added a little at a time, test it as in recipe 628, and add, if needed, a little egg white or cream.
The forcemeat can, if desired, be flavored with a little grated onion, finely chopped mushrooms or truffle, and the same amount of butter can be used instead of suet or lard.
Veal forcemeat can also be prepared as in recipes 628, 629 and 630.
Cook in a water bath or braise in an oven.
Forcemeat of pork can be prepared in the same way.

title: Färs av oxkött (Beef Forcemeat)
description: Prepared with beef, lard or kidney or fat, and egg yolk.

ingredients.name: 50 g. lard or cleaned kidney fat
2 hg. bread panade or 2 tbsp. flour (20 g.)
1/2 tbsp. butter (10 g.) for the onion
1/2 liter boiling broth or water, mixed with 1/2 tsp. solid meat extract

steps: Dry the meat with a cloth wrung out in hot water, and cut into cubes, removing all sinews and membranes carefully.
Scrape and cut the lard into pieces; if using kidney fat, chop it finely.
Mix the meat with the lard or kidney fat and the seasonings, and grind 6 times through a meat grinder.

Pound the forcemeat in a stone mortar together with the panade (see recipe no. 626) or flour, until it is smooth and supple, then place it in a bowl and add the beaten egg and egg yolk under vigorous stirring.
Continue stirring the forcemeat for about 3/4 hour while gradually adding the cream or milk.
Test it (see recipe no. 628); if it is too firm, add a little more cream; if too soft, add an egg white.
If desired, add lastly the onion that has been fried in butter.
Grease a long baking pan with cold butter, place the forcemeat in it and shape it as an oblong roll.
Brush it with the egg white and sprinkle with crushed rusks.
Put the forcemeat in the oven and brown it, basting it frequently with the butter in the pan.
When browned, dilute it with the boiling broth or water mixed with meat extract, and let it finish cooking, which takes about 1/2 hour.
During cooking, baste it about every 10 minutes.
Place the forcemeat on a hot platter, cut into thin slices, garnish with parsley and serve with the beaten, strained meat gravy or with a prepared sauce (see recipe no. 429).
If desired, use 3 hg. beef and 2 hg. veal, with the same amount of lard or kidney fat.
The forcemeat may be diluted with broth or water instead of cream or milk.
If the forcemeat is cooked in a water bath, dilute it with somewhat more cream.

title: Färserad gädda (Stuffed Pike)
description: Prepared with pike, cream, and white pepper.

ingredients.name: 1.4 kg pike (= 600 g scraped fish meat)

steps: Scale the pike and cut it open along the back, remove the innards and wash the fish well
Remove the backbone and carefully scrape the meat from the skin
Sew the skin together with a surgical stitch and leave a small opening at the head
Force the finely scraped fish meat together with butter three times through a meat grinder and then pound with the egg yolks in a mortar until the mass is fine and cohesive
In a bowl mix the flour, cream and seasonings
When everything is well mixed, work the mixture into the forcemeat tablespoon by tablespoon
Work the forcemeat for about 1 hour, then fold in the egg whites beaten to stiff peaks
Test the forcemeat and fill through a pastry tube into the prepared fish skin
The fish should not be overfilled as the forcemeat will swell from the beaten egg white and the fish may burst
Brush the pike with egg, sprinkle with crushed hardtack and bake in the oven for about 1 1/2 hours
Serve with mushroom, crayfish or lobster sauce

title: Färserad kalkon (Stuffed Turkey)
description: Prepared with turkey, truffles, and white pepper.
steps: Pluck the turkey preferably while it is warm, singe, draw, rinse well and dry (see page 299 et seq.), after which the breastbone is carefully cut out from inside.
Lard the breast and thighs thickly with finely cut truffle strips and let the turkey hang 2-6 days depending on the season.
The day before the turkey is to be roasted, prepare the chicken forcemeat. Pluck the hens, singe, draw (see page 299), rinse very well, dry with a cloth and skin them.
Cut all meat loose from the carcass, scrape free from sinews and membranes, mix with seasonings and pass 5 times through a meat grinder.
Pound it together with flour, with a wooden pestle, in a stone mortar until a fine mass.
Whip the eggs and add to the forcemeat, little by little, under vigorous stirring, after which it is left in a cool place until the next day.

Place the forcemeat in a saucepan set in a bowl with ice (it will separate otherwise when the cream is worked in) and add the cream teaspoon by teaspoon under even stirring, after which the truffles cut into fine strips or dice are added and the forcemeat is carefully tasted.
Dry the turkey with a damp cloth, rub inside and outside with seasonings, stuff with the chicken forcemeat, sew well with a surgical stitch, truss and cover with lard (see page 300).
Roast thereafter as in no. 606, slice beautifully and arrange on a platter so that it appears whole, garnish and serve as in no. 605.
The turkey can also be boiled as in no. 600 and served with truffle sauce.

title: Färserade järpar (Stuffed Grouse)
description: Prepared with grouse, chicken, and veal.
steps: Pluck and singe the grouse, carefully remove the head, wings and feet, but leave the bones. Cut them open along the back, remove the innards, rinse the birds well and dry them. Cut the meat loose from the breastbone as close to the skin as possible, without tearing it. Remove and rinse the chicken well and pluck it. Remove all meat from the bones and scrape it together with the grouse and veal meat, free of sinews and membranes.

Beat the meat well with the butter and eggs, and work the forcemeat for 1/2 hour, adding the cream little by little, together with the seasonings and flour. Pass the forcemeat through a fine sieve and mix with the truffles cut into strips, then place on ice to set.

When the forcemeat is set, fill it into the bird skins, which are shaped like grouse. Sew the skin together, cover the birds with lard slices, tie a mussel shell around each one. Place them in a flat pot with the breast up and cook in gentle broth for about 40 minutes.
Rinse the rice grains, add to boiling salted water and cook until tender, then drain in a colander and let drain well. Mix with the mustard and pack into a water-rinsed, smooth, round baking form.

For the gelatin, rinse it in cold water and dissolve in the hot broth, which is then poured onto a dish to set. Turn the rice bottom out onto a round serving dish and garnish with chopped gelatin, parsley, and place the lettuce head in the middle. Free the birds from the lard and thread with which they were sewn together and cut into beautiful slices, but so that they retain their form. Place them in indentations around the salad and garnish the arrangement with the cut tomatoes and the rest of the gelatin, cut into triangles with a small truffle slice on each triangle.
Serve the grouse as an entrée with brown gravy prepared from the roasted bird bones or with bird sauce, thinned with cream.
